source.title: Fine-tuning Aligned Language Models Compromises Safety, Even When Users Do Not Intend To!
source.venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) 2024 -- Oral

confidence_rationale: ICLR 2024 oral with a directly measured competence-vs-harm-sensitivity trade: fine-tuning on benign, utility-motivated data measurably degrades safety behaviour. Mapping fidelity is the strongest of any entry here because the paper's benign-dataset condition IS the claim's scenario -- an optimisation run whose only intent was competence, whose collateral cost was harm sensitivity. Held below 0.9 because the mechanism is gradient fine-tuning of a language model's alignment layer rather than a skill-refinement knob in an embodied agent, and because the paper measures one of INV-093's four axes (harm sensitivity) and says nothing about residue accumulation or commitment integrity.
failure_signatures: A refinement run undertaken with no adversarial intent, on ordinary utility data, degrades harm refusal behaviour as a side effect -- so benign intent is not a defence and cannot be used to argue a refinement mechanism is safe by construction.
Safety behaviour established before refinement does not survive refinement: an initially impeccable alignment provides no floor once the optimiser is allowed to move the weights that carry it.
The degradation is invisible to the competence metric the refinement was run against, so a single-axis acceptance test passes a mechanism that has broken the invariant.

mapping.source_claim_statement: The safety alignment of a large language model can be compromised by fine-tuning on a few adversarially designed examples, and -- separately -- fine-tuning on benign, commonly used datasets can also inadvertently degrade safety alignment, to a lesser but real extent.
mapping.ree_translation: The benign-dataset result is the empirical instance of INV-093's failure mode: an optimisation procedure aimed purely at competence silently attenuated the system's harm sensitivity, and the competence metric it was optimising registered success throughout. REE's skill-refinement mechanisms sit in the same structural position as this fine-tuning step -- they update the parameters that carry both skill and constraint -- so the paper is evidence that the non-degradation half of INV-093's acceptance shape has to be measured rather than assumed, and that measuring it requires a probe outside the competence objective.
mapping.mapping_caveat: The substrate is wrong in two ways that matter. (1) LLM safety alignment is a post-hoc behavioural layer over a pretrained model, not a structurally distinct harm channel of the kind REE posits; its fragility under gradient updates may say more about how shallowly alignment is encoded than about any general competence-vs-harm trade. (2) The paper has no refinement-strength sweep of the sort INV-093's falsifier specifies -- it compares conditions, not a continuum -- so it establishes that the trade OCCURS without characterising how it scales, which is what REE actually needs to set an acceptance threshold.
mapping.source_context: Fine-tuning of aligned LLMs (GPT-3.5 Turbo via the OpenAI fine-tuning API, and Llama-2-Chat) under three regimes: explicitly harmful examples, implicitly harmful identity-shifting examples, and benign utility datasets; safety measured by harmfulness rate on held-out harmful instructions.

confidence_components.notes: Source quality high: ICLR oral, widely replicated since, effect large and cheaply reproducible. Mapping fidelity high on the benign-fine-tuning arm specifically -- that arm is a direct instance of the claim -- and much lower on the adversarial arms, which are an attack model rather than the collateral-degradation phenomenon INV-093 is about. Transfer risk moderate: language-model alignment to embodied harm sensitivity is a real leap, but INV-093 is stated over 'any competence-refinement mechanism', so the claim's own generality is what is being tested here.
